say.text: A 24-year-old woman has early appendicitis. Her appendix lumen is blocked, and mucus is still being made inside it.
Which event in the chain comes first?

choices.label: Arterial thrombosis, so the wall ischaemia starts first
Luminal obstruction, with mucus still being secreted
Parietal peritoneum is involved before the lumen blocks
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what has to happen to the lumen before mucus can back up and pressure can rise.
Gangrene is the feared end, so it is tempting to start the story at the artery.
The artery fails only after rising pressure compromises it. It is a late step in the chain, not the start.
The order is obstruction, rising pressure, venous congestion, arterial compromise, then gangrene and perforation.

sure_note.text: You were sure the vessel starts it. The lumen closes before any vessel fails.

say.text: Yes. Obstruction starts the chain. The blocked lumen keeps secreting mucus, and the pressure then rises.
The right-sided pain is the one you can point to, so the peritoneum feels like the start.
Early distension gives visceral pain at T10, felt around the navel. The parietal peritoneum is involved later.
Obstruction, then distension with visceral pain, then parietal involvement that localises the pain to the RIF.

sure_note.text: You were sure the peritoneum starts it. Visceral pain comes first, and parietal involvement comes later.

say.text: A 30-year-old man tells you he vomited twice at breakfast, and his belly pain began after that. He has no fever yet.
How do you read this history?

choices.label: Appendicitis is less likely, as vomiting came before pain
Appendicitis is likelier, as vomiting usually opens the illness
The order of symptoms carries no weight, so the story is neutral
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about which symptom typically opens appendicitis, and what this man says came first.
Yes. Murphy's sequence is pain, then vomiting, then fever. Vomiting before pain argues against appendicitis.
Vomiting is an early symptom in many gut illnesses, so it feels like the usual opener.
In appendicitis the order is pain, then vomiting, then fever. Vomiting first argues against it.
Read the order before the symptom list. Here the order points away from appendicitis.

sure_note.text: You were sure vomiting opens the illness. In appendicitis it follows the pain.

say.text: Appendicitis is taught as a list of symptoms, and all of them occur eventually, so the sequence seems a detail.
Murphy's sequence is the order in which symptoms appear, and it is diagnostic. Vomiting before pain argues against appendicitis.
The order is part of the diagnosis: pain, then vomiting, then fever.

sure_note.text: You were sure the order does not matter. In appendicitis it does.

say.text: A 34-year-old man has migrating pain, anorexia, tenderness in the right iliac fossa and a raised total count. He has no nausea, no rebound, no fever and no left shift.
What is his Alvarado total?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Give each item its own weight. Only two items in the score carry 2 points.
Migration is the classic sign, so it feels as if it deserves the extra point.
Migration scores 1, as does rebound. Only RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2.
Migration 1, anorexia 1, RIF tenderness 2, leucocytosis 2, which is 6.

sure_note.text: You were sure migration scores 2. It scores 1.

say.text: A raised count is a lab value, so it feels like it should carry a single point.
Leucocytosis scores 2 in the Alvarado score, the same as tenderness in the right iliac fossa.
Migration 1, anorexia 1, RIF tenderness 2, leucocytosis 2, which is 6.

sure_note.text: You were sure leucocytosis counts 1. It counts 2.

say.text: Yes, 6. Migration and anorexia score 1 each, and RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2 each. A total of 6 sits between the cut-offs of 4 and 7, so the score alone does not settle it.
A 25-year-old woman has right-sided pain that is reproduced when the examiner internally rotates her flexed right hip. Nothing else is found.
Which explanation of this sign fits best?

choices.label: Psoas sign, since internal rotation is the psoas test
Obturator sign, which suggests a pelvic appendix
Obturator sign, which suggests a retrocaecal appendix
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which muscle does internal rotation of the flexed hip stretch, and which structure does the appendix then touch?
Both are right-hip tests that hurt on movement, so the two names blur together.
The psoas sign is pain on extension of the right hip, not on internal rotation.
Internal rotation of the flexed hip is the obturator sign, which suggests a pelvic appendix.

sure_note.text: You were sure internal rotation is the psoas test. The psoas test is extension.

say.text: Yes. Pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip is the obturator sign. It suggests a pelvic appendix touching obturator internus.
Retrocaecal is the commonest position, so it feels like the default answer for any sign.
The obturator sign points to a pelvic appendix. Retrocaecal goes with the psoas sign.
Match the manoeuvre to its position: obturator with pelvic, psoas with retrocaecal.

sure_note.text: You were sure the commonest position fits. Each sign points to its own position.

say.text: A medical student tells you: 'For Rovsing's sign, press the right iliac fossa, and the pain is felt on the left.' You want to correct him.
Which version of the sign is right?

choices.label: Press the right fossa; pain is felt in the left fossa
Press the left fossa; pain is felt in the right fossa
Press the left fossa; pain is felt in the left fossa
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Predict first: which fossa is pressed, and on which side is the pain reported?
Rovsing's sign sounds like pressing where the trouble is, so the pressure site is easy to set to the painful side.
The pressure goes on the left iliac fossa, and the pain is felt on the right.
Press the left iliac fossa and ask about the right.

sure_note.text: You were sure the pressure goes on the painful side. It goes on the left.

say.text: Yes. Pressure in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa. The student has reversed the sign.
Local tenderness is what you expect at the palpated site, so the pain seems to belong where the pressure is.
Rovsing's sign is pain felt away from the pressure, on the right side.
Left pressure, right pain. The pain is felt on the opposite side from the pressure.

sure_note.text: You were sure the pain stays under the fingers. In Rovsing's sign it moves to the other side.

say.text: A surgeon is counselling a patient before an appendicectomy and lists the risks of the operation and of the disease.
Which of these is a complication of the operation itself, not of the disease?

choices.label: Right groin bulge after femoral nerve injury
Generalised peritonitis after the appendix perforated
Right inguinal hernia after ilioinguinal nerve injury
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether the complication needs the knife to happen, or would occur from the disease alone.
A groin bulge makes you think of the femoral canal, so the femoral nerve comes to mind.
The nerve named for a gridiron incision is the ilioinguinal nerve, not the femoral nerve.
After a gridiron incision, injury to the ilioinguinal nerve can cause a right inguinal hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure the femoral nerve is the one at risk. It is the ilioinguinal nerve.

say.text: Peritonitis is the best-known complication of appendicitis, so it feels like a surgical one too.
Peritonitis follows perforation of the diseased appendix, before any operation.
Operative complications are wound infection, faecal fistula and nerve injury. Peritonitis belongs to the disease.

sure_note.text: You were sure peritonitis is an operative complication. It comes from the disease itself.

say.text: Yes. A gridiron incision can injure the ilioinguinal nerve and cause a right inguinal hernia. Peritonitis is a complication of the disease, from perforation.
A 66-year-old man has three weeks of right iliac fossa pain, weight loss and anaemia. Examination finds a firm mass in the right iliac fossa.
What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: Acute appendicitis, since RIF pain always means it
Appendicular mass, since any RIF mass is one
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the age, the three weeks of symptoms and the weight loss before you settle on the mass.
Yes. In older adults, caecal carcinoma is the key right iliac fossa look-alike. Appendicitis peaks in the second and third decades.
RIF pain with a mass looks like appendicitis, and appendicitis is the commonest surgical emergency of the abdomen.
Appendicitis peaks in the second and third decades. Age and weight loss shift the list of look-alikes towards caecal carcinoma.
Caecal carcinoma explains weeks of right-sided symptoms, anaemia and weight loss in an older man.

sure_note.text: You were sure RIF pain means appendicitis. In this age group a look-alike is the more likely answer.

say.text: Classic appendicular masses are felt in the RIF, so any mass there feels like one.
An appendicular mass usually forms after 3 to 5 days of symptoms. Three weeks with weight loss and anaemia does not fit it.
Sort the look-alikes by age: in the elderly, caecal carcinoma is the one to name first.

sure_note.text: You were sure any RIF mass is appendicular. The timing and the age point elsewhere.

say.text: A 26-year-old woman at 18 weeks of pregnancy has right iliac fossa pain. Her junior suggests a contrast CT, since CT is the most accurate test.
What do you order first?

choices.label: Contrast-enhanced CT first, as the most accurate test
MRI abdomen without gadolinium first, to avoid radiation
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which test is first-line in pregnancy, and which one is kept for when that test does not answer.
CT is the most accurate test in adults, so accuracy feels like the right first criterion.
In pregnancy, ultrasound is the first test. CT is not the first test in a pregnant woman.
The order is graded-compression ultrasound first, then MRI without gadolinium only if it is inconclusive.

sure_note.text: You were sure accuracy decides the first test. In pregnancy the first-line test is chosen for safety and availability.

say.text: Yes. Ultrasound is the first-line test in pregnancy. MRI without gadolinium is the second rung, used when ultrasound is inconclusive.
MRI gives good images without ionising radiation, so it feels like the safe first step.
MRI without gadolinium is the second rung in pregnancy, used when ultrasound is inconclusive.
The order is ultrasound first, then MRI only if the ultrasound is inconclusive.

sure_note.text: You were sure MRI comes first. In pregnancy it comes second.

say.text: A 24-year-old woman has right iliac fossa pain for 12 hours. The surgical team wants her in theatre this evening, and no pregnancy test has been sent.
What comes first before theatre?

choices.label: Theatre now, and send the pregnancy test with the swab
Serum or urine beta-hCG, before anything else
Ultrasound first, and the pregnancy test only if it is positive
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with the test that every woman of reproductive age needs before any scan or operation.
She needs theatre urgently, so every minute counts and the test seems able to wait.
Beta-hCG comes before any imaging or surgery in every woman of reproductive age, to exclude ectopic pregnancy.
Test first: beta-hCG, then decide on imaging or theatre.

sure_note.text: You were sure the test can wait. It comes before theatre.

say.text: Yes. Beta-hCG is needed in every woman of reproductive age, to exclude ectopic pregnancy, before imaging or surgery.
The scan answers the diagnosis, so it feels like the step to take first.
The pregnancy test is required before imaging, not conditional on what the scan shows.
Beta-hCG first in every woman of reproductive age, then the scan.

sure_note.text: You were sure the scan leads. The pregnancy test leads.

say.text: A 41-year-old accountant has two days of vague right iliac fossa pain. The ultrasound report says the appendix was not identified.
What is the best next step?

choices.label: Discharge with advice, as the scan did not show appendicitis
Repeat graded-compression ultrasound, the investigation of choice
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: A scan that did not see the appendix is not the same as one that excluded it. Ask which test is most accurate in adults.
A report with no appendicitis on it sounds like a clear result.
Not identified is not a negative scan. A negative ultrasound does not exclude appendicitis in an adult.
Persisting pain after an inconclusive scan needs contrast CT before any discharge.

sure_note.text: You were sure a clear report settles it. In an adult this report is not negative.

say.text: Ultrasound is the test most exam keys name first, so repeating it feels reasonable.
The older key named ultrasound as investigation of choice in general. In adults the most accurate test is contrast CT.
Ultrasound is first in children and pregnancy. In adults, contrast CT is the most accurate.

sure_note.text: You were sure the older key applies to adults. In adults the answer is CT.

say.text: Yes. In adults contrast-enhanced CT is the most accurate test, and it shows abscess, perforation and appendicolith.
A 47-year-old fit woman has CT-proven uncomplicated appendicitis. There is no abscess, no perforation and no appendicolith. She asks whether she must have surgery.
What do you tell her?

choices.label: Appendicectomy is the only treatment, so surgery is the only offer
Antibiotics-first is an accepted option, with surgery if it fails
Antibiotics-first, even though the scan shows a small abscess
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Check what the scan shows against the words 'uncomplicated' and 'no appendicolith' before you answer.
Appendicectomy is the textbook answer, so 'only treatment' feels like a safe absolute.
PYQs expected appendicectomy as the only treatment. Current practice accepts antibiotics-first for selected CT-proven uncomplicated adults.
Offer both: appendicectomy as the treatment of choice, and antibiotics-first as an accepted option for selected patients.

sure_note.text: You were sure the textbook 'only' applies. It is the older key.

say.text: Yes. For selected CT-proven uncomplicated disease, antibiotics-first is accepted, and appendicectomy follows if the antibiotics fail.
Antibiotics are the first step for most infections, so a small abscess seems no barrier.
Antibiotics-first is for uncomplicated disease. An abscess is complicated, and it is drained.
Drain an abscess and treat it. Offer antibiotics-first only for uncomplicated disease with no appendicolith.

sure_note.text: You were sure antibiotics are safe with an abscess. It is complicated.

say.text: Two patients are on your ward. One has a settling appendicular mass. The other has an appendicular abscess that is drainable on CT.
Which pairing of problem and first treatment is right?

choices.label: Mass: Ochsner-Sherren regimen. Abscess: image-guided drainage
Mass: immediate appendicectomy. Abscess: open drainage
Mass: routine interval appendicectomy at 6-8 weeks. Abscess: drainage
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which of the two needs to settle before any operation, and which needs a drain?
Yes. The mass is managed conservatively with the Ochsner-Sherren regimen. The abscess is drained percutaneously under image guidance, with antibiotics.
A mass that will not settle feels like a surgical problem, and an abscess seems to need an incision.
The mass is managed conservatively first. Open drainage is for when percutaneous drainage fails or is unavailable.
Mass: regimen first. Abscess: image-guided drainage with antibiotics.

sure_note.text: You were sure open surgery is first. The mass is conservative first.

say.text: The classic exam answer is interval appendicectomy at 6 to 8 weeks, so the pairing feels right.
Current practice makes interval surgery selective, with colonoscopy or CT first in older patients.
Mass: conservative regimen first, then surgery only if the patient is selected.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the textbook timing. Current practice makes it selective.

say.text: A pathologist reports on an appendix removed for a long-standing complaint. She asks which tumour is commonest in the appendix.
Which is the commonest tumour of the appendix?
A tumour-like swelling full of mucus looks like the commonest growth in the appendix.
A mucocele may rupture and cause pseudomyxoma peritonei, but it is not the commonest tumour.
Carcinoid, the neuroendocrine tumour, is the commonest tumour of the appendix.

sure_note.text: You were sure the mucus lesion is commonest. It is a lesion, not the commonest tumour.

say.text: Yes. Carcinoid is the commonest appendix tumour and usually sits at the tip. PYQs expect the size rule: under 2 cm at the tip, appendicectomy alone; over 2 cm, right hemicolectomy.
Caecal cancer is common in older patients, so the appendix seems likely to follow the same pattern.
Caecal carcinoma is an elderly right iliac fossa look-alike, but the commonest appendix tumour is carcinoid.
Carcinoid, a neuroendocrine tumour, usually at the tip, is the commonest.

sure_note.text: You were sure the appendix follows the caecum. Carcinoid is the commonest appendix tumour.
